t: Overview: outline and place in the book
n: In this lecture we will consider the instrumental methods of chemical-toxicological analysis. Remember: in the book the instrumental methods are not in a separate chapter; they are scattered within the topics on alkaloids, pesticides and medicinal substances. The overview covers the following methods: UV spectrophotometry, photoelectrocolorimetry (PEC), thin-layer chromatography (TLC), gas-liquid chromatography (GLC), high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), gel chromatography, microcrystalloscopy and thermal desorption surface ionisation spectroscopy (TDSIS). Key terms: spectrophotometry, photocolorimetry, chromatography, retention time and detection limit.

Chemical-toxicological analysis is carried out in two stages. The first stage is isolation and purification of toxic substances. The second stage is determination of the quality and quantity of the isolated substance. In detecting poisons, a preliminary tentative examination and analytical screening methods are used. Detecting an unknown poison in a biological specimen takes a long time. Therefore, to speed up the analysis, external signs and tentative methods are important. The sequence: tentative examination, isolation and purification, determination of quality, that is identity, then determination of quantity.

Tentative methods, although highly sensitive, are not specific. Sometimes they detect a substance even at a therapeutic dose. Therefore the result must be confirmed by an additional method. On the basis of G.M. Radionova's method, 49 medicinal substances are distinguished in various systems and on various sorbents. V.A. Kartoshov proposed distinguishing 83 nitrogen-containing organic toxic compounds on the basis of 5 standard substances. And the TLC screening method developed by the staff of the department makes it possible to detect and distinguish organophosphorus compounds.

Now the principle of UV spectrophotometry. Spectrophotometry is based on measuring monochromatic radiation in the visible and the adjacent ultraviolet region. The dependence of light absorption on wavelength is called the absorption spectrum of a substance. Absorbance is measured at the wavelength corresponding to the maximum absorption of the solution under study. That is, the spectrum is first recorded, then the maximum is found, and the measurement is made precisely at that wavelength.

About absorbance and the reference solution. The concentration is chosen so that the absorbance of the solution lies in the range from 0.2 to 1.0. When measuring the absorbance of only one substance in a mixture, the solution under study is placed in one cuvette and all the other components in the second. The solution in the second cuvette is called the reference solution. This means that the influence of components other than the substance being measured is excluded.

The measurement procedure in UV spectrophotometry consists of five steps. The first step is to prepare a solution at a concentration giving an absorbance of 0.2-1.0. The second is to record the spectrum, since the absorption spectrum depends on wavelength. The third is to find the maximum: the measuring wavelength corresponds to the maximum absorption. The fourth is to prepare the reference solution, that is the remaining components in the second cuvette. The fifth is to measure the absorbance and calculate the result.

t: Example: determination of caffeine by UV spectrophotometry
n: As an example, let us consider the determination of caffeine by UV spectrophotometry. To prepare the standard, 0.1 g of caffeine is dissolved in ethyl alcohol in a 100 ml volumetric flask. The spectrum is measured at 200-400 nm. The solution in ethyl alcohol has a maximum at 273 nm. The absorbance of caffeine from the specimen is measured at 273 nm, with ethyl alcohol used as the reference solution. Finally, the quantity is calculated from the absorbance D of the specimen isolate.

Examples of UV maxima. A solution of caffeine in ethyl alcohol gives a maximum at 273 nm, and a solution of theophylline in 0.1 M HCl at 270 nm. A solution of nicotine in 0.1 N H2SO4 gives a maximum at 260 nm. Indometacin absorbs with a maximum at 278 nm and diclofenac at 272 and 275 nm, with a 96% ethyl alcohol medium used. As can be seen, the maximum depends both on the substance and on the solvent medium.

The Bouguer-Lambert-Beer law: under the same conditions the absorbance of a solution is directly proportional to its concentration. Pyrethroids obey the general Bouguer-Lambert-Beer law in the concentration range of 10-100 µg/ml. Unlike photocolorimetry, spectrophotometry works more accurately over a wide range of wavelengths and in monochromatic light. The law holds only under the same conditions, that is when measured in the same cuvette.

The structure of a spectrophotometer. The main parts of the instrument: a light source, a monochromator or light filter, cuvettes, a detector and an indicator. In the ultraviolet region, deuterium and hydrogen lamps are used. In the visible and near-infrared region, ordinary tungsten lamps are used. In the SF-4, a dispersing prism works in the range 200-1100 nm. In the SFD-2, a diffraction grating works in the range 220-1100 nm.

Let us compare photocolorimetry and spectrophotometry. Photocolorimetry is based on analysing a substance by measuring it in the visible part of the spectrum under polychromatic radiation. Here the absorption maximum of the coloured solution and the absorption minimum of the light filter must coincide. Spectrophotometry, on the other hand, is based on measuring monochromatic radiation in the visible and adjacent ultraviolet region, and the measurement is made at the maximum. The difference is that in PEC a light filter is chosen, and in SF a wavelength.

The principle of the PEC method. Photocolorimetry is based on analysing a substance by measuring it in the visible part of the spectrum under polychromatic radiation. The absorption maximum of the coloured solution and the absorption minimum of the light filter must coincide. Example: the identity of novocaine is checked in PEC by the azo dye reaction. Here the maximum absorption is measured with different light filters.

t: Methods of quantitative calculation in PEC and SF
n: In PEC and spectrophotometry there are several methods of quantitative calculation. The first is the comparison method: Cx = Cst * Dx / Dst, in which absorbances are compared in a cuvette of the same thickness. The second is the calibration graph: a graph is plotted from the absorbance of several standard solutions and the unknown concentration is found. The third is the standard addition method: Cx = Ca * Dx / (D(x+a) - Dx); it reduces the negative influence of impurities. In addition, the differential method and extraction-photometric analysis are also used.

Extraction photometry and examples of PEC. Diphenhydramine, that is dimedrol, is determined in PEC by the extraction-photometric method in the presence of the indicator chrome black. Anabasine with KCN and chloramine B forms glutaconic aldehyde; the yellow-brown colour formed with barbituric acid is measured in PEC. Novocaine, in turn, is determined in PEC on the basis of the azo dye reaction.

Now we turn to chromatographic methods. Among chromatographic methods, thin-layer chromatography, column gel chromatography and paper chromatography are the most widely used. These methods make it possible not only to purify a substance from foreign impurities but also to establish the identity of the substance under examination. For this, various mobile systems, sorbents and visualising reagents are used. TLC stands for thin-layer chromatography.

Examples of TLC systems. System for barbiturates: chloroform - n-butanol - 25% NH4OH, ratio 70:40:5. The reagent used is 0.02% diphenylcarbazone in chloroform and mercury sulphate; ink-coloured spots are formed. For alkaloids: chloroform-acetone-diethylamine, ratio 50:30:2, or chloroform-acetone-ammonia, ratio 30:20:2; the visualising agent is Dragendorff reagent. System for caffeine: ether-acetone-25% ammonia, ratio 40:20:1; when sprayed with iodine solution and alcohol-HCl, a violet spot is formed.

Examples of Rf values in TLC. Nicotine: hexane-acetone, ratio 4:1, with acidified iodoplatinate Rf = 0.4, blue spot. Dimedrol: chloroform-acetone-25% ammonia, ratio 12:24:1, Rf = 0.58-0.60; benzhydrol 0.76-0.80. For NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) a chloroform-methanol system at a ratio of 9:1 is used: diclofenac 0.47; indometacin 0.38; ibuprofen 0.54. By Rf, a substance occupies its own position in the system.

A brief word on the history of chromatography. Chromatography was first applied in 1903 by M.S. Tswett to separate a complex mixture obtained from green plants. In 1941 Martin and Synge proposed paper chromatography and received the Nobel Prize; they also indicated a gas as a mobile phase. In 1952 James and Martin developed the methods of gas-adsorption and gas-liquid chromatography.

The principle of GLC. If the mobile phase is a gas and the stationary phase is a high-boiling liquid, the method is called gas-liquid chromatography, that is GLC. The liquid sorbent is impregnated onto a solid neutral material. GLC is the redistribution and separation of substances between a gas and a liquid. The separation of substances is explained by the distribution coefficient K. If K is small, the substance leaves the column quickly.

A gas chromatograph consists of the following parts: a gas source, a reducer, a sample-quantity meter, a chromatographic column, detectors, an oven, an injector and a recording device. The carrier gas, for example nitrogen or argon, is introduced into the column together with the sample. The column, injector and detector are located in the oven. The injector has a rubber septum, and the sample is introduced with a microsyringe. The vaporiser temperature is about 50 °C higher than the column temperature.

GLC detectors. The detector converts a change in the composition of the gas leaving the column into an electrical impulse, and a chromatogram is obtained on the recorder. Types: katharometer, flame ionisation, electron capture and thermionic detectors. The katharometer measures the difference in thermal conductivity between pure carrier gas and the mixture with the substance. The flame ionisation detector measures the current produced by ionisation of organic substances in a hydrogen flame.

Retention time and qualitative analysis. The main characteristic of a substance is its retention time or distance in the column, that is the time from injection to the peak maximum. The true retention time equals the difference between the total time and the dead retention time, tm: ttrue = ttotal - tm. In qualitative analysis, retention parameters and comparison with a standard are used, chemical reactions are carried out before or after chromatography, and the method is also used together with UV, IR, mass spectrometry and NMR.

In GLC the quantity is determined in three ways: internal standard, absolute calibration and internal normalisation. Advantages: the method is universal, separates complex mixtures into components, the analysis is rapid and sensitive, and little substance is required. Accuracy is high, with a relative error of ±1.0-1.5%. The disadvantage is the volatility and instability of some liquid stationary phases.

t: GLC: determination of alcohols via alkyl nitrites
n: Determination of alcohols by GLC by means of alkyl nitrites. Alcohols from blood and urine are converted into alkyl nitrites and chromatographed, because alkyl nitrites are several times more volatile than the corresponding alcohols. To form the alkyl nitrite, trichloroacetic acid is placed in a penicillin vial, then blood or urine, and sodium nitrite is added. The quantity is determined by the internal standard method; the internal standard is propyl alcohol. The calculation is made from the ratio of the peak heights of ethyl nitrite and propyl nitrite.

An example of practical GLC conditions. Column: a 130 x 0.2 cm glass column packed with Chromaton N-AW-DMCS impregnated with 5% SE-30; carrier gas nitrogen, 30 ml/min. The oven temperature is raised from 180 to 220 °C at 10 °C/min, then to 245 °C at 3 °C/min. Detector temperature 260 °C, injector 250 °C. The retention times of synthetic pyrethroids are given in the table; under these conditions they are analysed by GLC.

High-performance liquid chromatography, that is HPLC. Here the mobile phase, the eluent, passes through the sorbent in the column at high speed under high pressure. The method makes it possible to separate high- and low-molecular-weight, heat-labile substances and to determine their identity and quantity. Parts of the instrument: a high-performance column, an injector, a high-pressure pump, a detector with a recording device, and a microprocessor.

The pump, column and detectors of HPLC. The high-pressure pump gives a pressure of up to 200-500 atm; in microcolumn chromatographs 1-20 atm. Columns are made of stainless steel or glass, 10-25 cm long, with an internal diameter of 0.3-0.8 cm; the adsorbent particle size is 5-10 µm. Detectors: refractometric, fluorimetric, spectrophotometric with variable wavelength, 190-900 nm, or fixed, 254 nm, mass spectrometric and others. The adsorbent is most often silica gel with hydroxyl groups, aluminium oxide and polymers.

Qualitative and quantitative analysis in HPLC. The quantity is determined from the chromatogram by absolute calibration or the internal standard method. In the same medium a substance leaves the column at the same constant time; this property is used to establish identity. In quantitative analysis the peak area is calculated, since the area is directly proportional to the quantity of the substance. So time indicates identity, and area indicates quantity.

Practical examples of HPLC. Zorbax Eclipse XDB C18 column, 150 x 4.6 mm, 5 µm, pH 3.0 buffer-acetonitrile, 210 nm. Retention times, in minutes: glipizide 8.45; gliclazide 9.97; glibenclamide 11.73; gliquidone 14.58. Pyrethroids are analysed at 278-280 nm in 24 minutes: danitol 17.4; cypermethrin 18.7 and 19.7; decis 20.1 minutes.

Gel chromatography. Here the same solvent is used as both the mobile and the stationary phase. The pores of the gel particles let small molecules through; large molecules pass between the particles and are washed out first, the small ones later. The mixture is separated depending on the volume and mass of the molecules. The method is simple, rapid and carried out under mild conditions.

Gels and their types. Gels are divided into soft, semi-rigid and rigid gels; each may be hydrophilic or hydrophobic. Semi-rigid gels consist of copolymers of styrene and divinylbenzene, that is styragels; on swelling the volume increases 1.1-1.8 times. Rigid gels include silica gel, that is porasil, and porous glass. Their disadvantages are the hydroxyl groups and high leachability.

Application of gel chromatography. Gels were first applied by Porath and Flodin in 1959 for liquid mixtures. The method is used in two forms, column and thin-layer. The internal diameter of the glass tube is 8-10 mm; increasing the diameter to 50 mm raises efficiency, while decreasing it is not recommended.

Let us dwell on microcrystalloscopy using nicotine as an example. With Dragendorff reagent, nicotine forms reddish crystals in the shape of X and K; the detection limit is 1 µg. With Reinecke salt, nicotine gives prismatic red-pink crystals; the detection limit is 1.2 µg. Anabasine and coniine also form crystals with Dragendorff reagent, but the shape of the crystals differs.

Other examples of microcrystalloscopy. Ethylene glycol is converted into calcium oxalate crystals; under the microscope the crystals appear envelope-shaped; the sensitivity of the reaction equals 0.1 g of ethylene glycol. The crystals dissolve under the action of mineral acids; in some cases the crystal shape forms after 2-3 days. Colour reagents may lead to a false conclusion with foreign substances. Therefore a microcrystalloscopic reaction and a pharmacological test are recommended.

Microcrystalloscopic determination of ethylene glycol. Ethylene glycol is converted into calcium oxalate crystals. The reaction is based on oxidation to oxalic acid; the reagents used are concentrated HNO3 and CaCl2 with NH4OH. In the precipitate on the slide, characteristic crystals resembling an envelope are seen; in some cases the shape forms after 2-3 days. The crystals dissolve under the action of mineral acids; the sensitivity of the reaction equals 0.1 g of ethylene glycol.

TDSIS, that is thermal desorption surface ionisation spectroscopy, is a new method with high sensitivity: very small amounts of substance are determined. It makes it possible to analyse nanoquantities of nitrogen-containing molecules and their metabolites with an accuracy of 1·10-11 g without chromatographic separation. Principle: the molecules are vaporised at a programmed temperature and recorded in a surface ionisation detector as a thermal desorption spectrum.

The analytical conditions of TDSIS. Emitter: oxidised molybdenum with iridium alloy; emitter voltage 405 V; emitter temperature 390-420 °C. Vaporisation temperature from room temperature to 505 °C; air flow 50 l/h; sample volume 1.0 µl. Qualitative analysis is carried out by the effective desorption temperatures. The spectrum of the specimen is compared with the reference spectrum in the computer databank.

Let us compare the chromatographic methods. In TLC the mobile phase is a mixture of solvents, that is a system; with different mobile systems, sorbents and visualising reagents, purification and identification can be carried out; assessment is by Rf. In GLC the mobile phase is a gas, and the main indicator is the retention time in the column. In HPLC the eluent passes under high pressure; the indicators are retention time and peak area. In gel chromatography the same solvent is used for both phases, and separation proceeds by molecular size.

Conclusion and choice of methods. Screening and tentative methods give speed but are not specific, so additional methods are needed for confirmation. Chromatographic methods, TLC, GLC and HPLC, perform separation and determination together; gel chromatography separates by molecular size. UV-SF and PEC are used in quantitative determination. Microcrystalloscopy supplements colour reactions, and TDSIS determines very small amounts without separation.
